The Qur'an. The central religious text of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the literal word of God, Allah, revealed orally to the Prophet Muhammad over roughly 23 years, from 609 to 632 CE. It is the foundation of Islamic theology, law, and practice.

The Qur'an is composed of 114 chapters, called surahs, each divided into verses called ayahs, totaling roughly 77,000 words in Arabic. It is written in Classical Arabic with a rhythmic, poetic structure called saj, which makes it aesthetically distinct from prose and verse. Muhammad received revelations orally and communicated them to followers, who memorized and wrote them on various materials. The standardized written compilation occurred under the third Caliph Uthman, around 650 CE.

The chapters are organized roughly by length, with the longest chapters first, rather than chronologically. Scholars distinguish between Meccan revelations, which are spiritual and shorter, and Medinan revelations, which address legal matters and are longer. This geographical and thematic division helps interpret the text's development.

Central themes include tawhid, monotheism; divine justice; prophetic tradition; ethical conduct; social justice; and the Day of Judgment. Muslims believe the Qur'an is inimitable—they call this i'jaz—and cannot be truly translated. Recitation in Arabic is integral to Islamic ritual. The text has been extensively commented upon, or tafsiered, by Islamic scholars across centuries, generating a vast body of interpretive tradition.

The Qur'an recognizes previous revelations—it honors Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. The Prophet Muhammad received these revelations from God, which Muslims believe constitute the literal word of Allah. The foundational scripture defines Islamic belief and practice, shaping the faith for over thirteen centuries.
